text: The last three lessons gave you real, working portability patterns — Kubernetes workloads, application-level interfaces over queues and databases, Terraform modules that branch by cloud. Every one of those works because the underlying capability genuinely exists on every cloud in a comparable form. This lesson is the honest other half: a real list of what doesn't work that way, and when to stop pretending it does.

Azure Cognitive Services' prebuilt models don't have a drop-in AWS equivalent at the same feature granularity — Textract and Rekognition solve adjacent problems with different APIs and accuracy characteristics, so abstracting between them means maintaining two genuinely different integrations, not one interface with thin adapters. DynamoDB's global-table consistency model has no true substitute either — Cosmos DB is comparably capable, but its consistency levels, pricing, and partitioning differ enough that tuned code won't perform or cost the same across the two. Step Functions and Logic Apps both orchestrate workflows, but porting one to the other is a rewrite, not a config change. And inside Kubernetes, depending directly on AKS's Azure Monitor integration or EKS's CloudWatch integration quietly exits the portable core from lesson nine.

None of that is a knock on these services — they're often the best tool for the job precisely because of that deep integration. The real failure mode is building an abstraction layer around one anyway, with no actual plan to run on a second cloud. Before doing that, ask one honest question: would you tolerate rewriting this specific integration if you switched clouds? If yes, stop — a possible future rewrite is cheaper than maintaining a multi-cloud abstraction today, indefinitely, for a migration that may never happen.

That leads to a practical portability budget instead of an all-or-nothing policy. Spend the discipline from this chapter on the actual application workload and the handful of commodity services with real equivalents everywhere — object storage, a relational database, a basic queue. Don't spend it on Cognitive Services, DynamoDB's specific behavior, or Step Functions and Logic Apps, because there's no honest equivalent to abstract toward, and the result would just be a worse, generic version of the exact feature you picked that service for.

That closes out chapter three. You've now got the real shape of workload portability: Kubernetes as the genuine layer, application interfaces over the services a workload depends on, multi-cloud Terraform modules to provision it all, and — just as important — a clear-eyed line on where chasing more of it stops being engineering and starts being wasted effort.
